chapter: Childhood, family and the sounds of New Orleans
title: Father Moses Barker and the mule on the dray
summary: His father was an unskilled laborer driving a dray with a mule that embarrassed him at Canal and St. Charles, one reason he went into the fast life.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Moses Barker. What did he do, Danny?
What did he do? He was a common laborer. Not exactly a common laborer, but he worked at any kind of job you can get. He didn't finish high school...

Yeah, unskilled. His last job was driving a dray truck, which was called a float. It's a peculiar early instrument to have drawn by mules or horses, or one horses... There was a float, a flatback, like you have the flatback trucks... It was a flatback, heavily constructed, low-slung, flatbedded vehicle that could hold maybe a ton.
Did it have two wheels or four wheels?
Because some drays had two wheels, didn't they.

Yeah. Yeah. This was a long thing, and it could bear... It could carry like four huge barrels of cotton. It could carry like eight barrels of wine, which was a variety of wine that you would bring to barrooms and what you call grog shops, which there was many of them in New Orleans, because this is a town that doesn't have a curfew -- so there were many wine-houses, called honky-tonks [hunky-tunks] and dives.

And he drove this truck, I mean what they called a float. And his work-mate was a white mule who was very inconvenient, who would decide to move his bowels right in the main part of town, which embarrassed my father, who sat on this wagon. He had to go through this procedure. The

mule would never wait for him to get back in the stable or in some sparsely settled area. He'd wait and get right at the corner of Canal and St. Charles (that's like at 50th and Broadway), and stop -- and you couldn't move him. And he would do his business right there. My father would sit there and have to go through this scene. It was very embarrassing.

This mule seemed to have a grievance against my father. Because when he got involved with the Nightlife People, people used to kid him. Every time they noticed what this mule was doing. Because different mules... Mules were very... They were as popular as people. Mules live a long life for animals. Certain people had certain wagons, and they had certain animals, and people admired the animals. "That's Willie's mule" or "That's Sam's horse" or "That horse belongs to that wagon." If they saw the kid bringing the mule or the horse to the blacksmith's shop, they could tell. They knew these animals, like they knew so-and-so's car. If you knew a kid had a goat and a little wagon, you knew that was little Willie's wagon and his goat.
That was the scene. That's part of the reason why my father went into the fast life.
